subject: 英語
title: 慶應義塾大学 商学部 英語 予想模試
coverNotes: 試験開始の合図があるまで、この問題冊子を開いてはいけません。
この問題冊子は、表紙を除き本文が全部で I から VII まであります。落丁、乱丁、印刷不鮮明の箇所等があった場合は、手を挙げて監督者に知らせてください。
解答は、すべて別紙の解答用紙に記入してください。マーク解答用紙と記述解答用紙の2種類があります。
マーク解答用紙には、HBの黒鉛筆を使用し、所定の解答欄の該当する番号を濃く正確にマークしてください。訂正する場合は、消しゴムできれいに消してください。
記述解答用紙には、所定の解答欄に、はっきりと記入してください。
解答用紙の受験番号欄・氏名欄は必ず記入してください。
問題冊子の余白は、適宜下書きに使用してかまいません。
disclaimer: 本模試は、過去の出題形式を参考に独自に作成したオリジナル問題です。慶應義塾大学および同大学の入学試験とは一切関係がありません。

sections.label: I
sections.instruction: 次の英文を読み、設問に答えなさい。解答はマーク解答用紙の 1 から 10 の解答欄にマークしなさい。

paragraphs: When a ride-hailing app charges twice the usual fare on a rainy Friday night, many customers feel cheated. Yet the same customers rarely complain when an airline charges more for a seat booked the day before departure, or when a hotel raises its rates during a popular festival. The practice behind all three cases is known as dynamic pricing: the adjustment of prices in response to changes in demand, supply, or other market conditions. {{b:1}} the idea is hardly new — street vendors have always raised their prices when crowds gather — digital technology has transformed its speed and scale.

Economists generally defend dynamic pricing on grounds of efficiency. A fixed price, they argue, sends no signal when conditions change. If fares stay the same during a storm, more people want rides than there are drivers willing to work, and the result is long waits for everyone. A higher price, by contrast, does two things at once: it {{b:2}} some riders to postpone trips that are not urgent, and it attracts additional drivers onto the road. In this view, the price is not a penalty imposed on unlucky customers but a piece of information that helps match buyers and sellers.

Consumers, however, do not always reason like economists. Research in behavioral economics suggests that people judge prices not only by how much they pay but by whether the price seems fair. In a well-known series of surveys, respondents were asked about a hardware store that raised the price of snow shovels on the morning after a heavy snowstorm. A large majority described the increase as unfair, even though it was exactly what a simple model of supply and demand would predict. {{u:5|What mattered to them was the reason behind the change}}: a firm passing on higher costs was usually forgiven, whereas a firm exploiting a sudden rise in need was not.

This sense of fairness places real limits on what firms can do. When a large online retailer was found, around the turn of the century, to be charging different customers different prices for the same DVD, the public reaction was so {{b:3}} that the company quickly apologized and refunded the difference. The episode illustrated a distinction that customers seem to draw instinctively. Prices that change over time, for everyone at once, are tolerated; prices that differ from person to person, for no visible reason, provoke anger.

The arrival of artificial intelligence has made this distinction harder to maintain. Algorithms can now estimate, from a customer's location, device, and purchase history, roughly how much that particular person is willing to pay. In principle, a company could use such estimates to offer each shopper an individual price — a strategy economists call "first-degree price discrimination." Supporters point out that this need not harm everyone: students or low-income customers might be offered discounts they would never receive under a single price. Critics reply that the practice {{u:6|tilts the informational balance firmly in the seller's favor}}, since a customer cannot see what others are paying and therefore cannot tell whether a deal is a good one.

Regulators in several countries have begun to respond. Some proposals would require firms to disclose when a price has been personalized; others would ban the use of certain data, such as health information, in setting prices. {{b:4}}, many businesses have concluded that transparency is in their own interest. Some ride-hailing services now show customers, before they book, how much the current fare exceeds the usual one, and offer to notify them when it falls. Such measures do not change the underlying economics, but they appear to reduce the feeling of being taken advantage of.

The debate over dynamic pricing, then, is less about whether prices should move than about who benefits when they do. A price that rises during a storm may put more cars on the road, but if customers come to believe that the system is designed mainly to extract as much money from them as possible, they may simply turn to competitors — or to their own cars. In the long run, firms that rely on flexible pricing may find that their most valuable asset is not the cleverness of their algorithms but the trust of the people who use them.
notes: snow shovel 雪かき用シャベル

groups.instruction: 設問A　空所（1）〜（4）に入る最も適切な語句を、それぞれ選択肢 1〜4 から1つ選びなさい。

questions.explanation: 「その考え自体は新しくない」と「デジタル技術が速度と規模を一変させた」は対比の関係。譲歩の Although が入る。
高い料金は、急ぎでない乗車を先送りするよう一部の利用者を「促す」。oblige（義務づける）は強すぎ、permit（許す）は文脈上「価格が延期を許可する」となり不自然。
so ... that 構文で「会社がすぐに謝罪し返金した」ほどの反応なので、「敵意に満ちた（hostile）」が適切。
規制当局の動き（前文）と並行して企業側も透明性を重視し始めた、という同時進行の関係。Meanwhile（一方で、その間に）が入る。因果関係はないので Therefore は不可。

groups.instruction: 設問B　下線部（5）・（6）の意味・内容として最も適切なものを、それぞれ選択肢 1〜4 から1つ選びなさい。

questions.prompt: 下線部（5）
choices: People cared mostly about the size of a price increase.
People judged a price increase according to why it happened.
People believed that shops should never change their prices.
People were unable to explain their reactions to price changes.
questions.explanation: 直後のコロン以下で「コスト転嫁なら許されるが、需要の急増につけ込むのは許されない」と説明されている。値上げの「理由」で判断する、という 2 が正解。

questions.prompt: 下線部（6）
choices: It gives sellers more knowledge about the transaction than buyers have.
It forces sellers to share their data with buyers.
It makes prices easier for buyers to compare.
It reduces the amount of data that sellers collect.
questions.explanation: since 以下「客は他人がいくら払っているか分からない」から、情報面で売り手が優位になるという意味。1 が正解。

groups.instruction: 設問C　本文の内容に照らして、（7）〜（9）の英文を完成させる、または質問に答えるのに最も適切なものを、それぞれ選択肢 1〜4 から1つ選びなさい。

questions.prompt: According to the second paragraph, economists believe that keeping fares fixed during a storm would
choices: reduce the number of drivers who stop working.
lead to a shortage of rides and long waits.
make customers feel that they were treated fairly.
encourage riders to book their trips earlier.
questions.explanation: 第2段落「料金が変わらなければ、乗りたい人が働く運転手より多くなり、全員が長く待つことになる」。2 が正解。

questions.prompt: The example of the snow shovels is used to show that
choices: most stores raise their prices after natural disasters.
economic models cannot predict how prices change.
people's sense of fairness can conflict with standard economic reasoning.

questions.explanation: 需給モデル通りの値上げなのに大多数が「不公平」と答えた例。公平感が経済学の標準的な考え方と食い違うことを示している。

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which kind of pricing do customers find most acceptable?
choices: Prices that differ for each customer depending on browsing history.
Prices that change over time but are the same for everyone at a given moment.
Prices that are set according to customers' health information.
Prices that are kept secret until after a purchase is made.
questions.explanation: 第4段落「時間とともに全員一斉に変わる価格は容認され、人によって理由なく異なる価格は怒りを招く」。2 が正解。

groups.instruction: 設問D　本文の内容と一致するものを、選択肢 1〜5 から1つ選び、解答番号（10）にマークしなさい。

choices: Dynamic pricing was first invented as a result of digital technology.
Supporters of personalized pricing argue that some customers could benefit from it.
Regulators in all countries have banned the use of personal data in setting prices.
Showing customers the size of a fare increase has changed the economics of ride-hailing.
The author concludes that algorithms are a firm's most valuable asset.
questions.explanation: 第5段落「支持者は、学生や低所得者が割引を受けられる可能性を指摘する」と一致。1 は第1段落（考え自体は昔からある）、3 は「一部の国」、4 は「根本的な経済性は変わらない」、5 は「最も価値ある資産は信頼」に反する。

sections.label: II
sections.instruction: 次の英文を読み、設問に答えなさい。解答はマーク解答用紙の 11 から 20 の解答欄にマークしなさい。

paragraphs: In April 1956, a converted oil tanker called the Ideal X left the port of Newark, New Jersey, carrying fifty-eight large metal boxes on its deck. Few people paid attention. The ship's owner, a trucking businessman named Malcom McLean, was not trying to change the world; he was trying to {{b:11}} the traffic jams that slowed his trucks along the crowded highways of the East Coast. His solution was simple: rather than unloading goods from a truck, carrying them onto a ship piece by piece, and loading them onto another truck at the other end, why not lift the entire trailer body onto the ship?

Before the container, loading and unloading a ship was slow, expensive, and dangerous work. Cargo arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels, crates, and bales of every size, and gangs of dockworkers had to fit each item into the ship's hold by hand. A vessel could spend nearly as much time in port as it did at sea. Theft was common, and damage more common still. By some estimates, the cost of handling cargo at the docks made up {{b:12}} half the total cost of moving goods across the ocean.

The container changed all of this by making cargo uniform. Once goods were packed into a standard box at a factory, they did not need to be touched again until they reached their final destination. Cranes could lift the boxes on and off ships in minutes, and the same box could travel by ship, train, and truck without ever being opened. McLean's first voyage reportedly reduced the cost of loading from almost six dollars per ton to about sixteen cents. {{u:15|Numbers like these}} were impossible for the rest of the industry to ignore.

Yet the container did not succeed overnight. For more than a decade, shipping lines, railways, and ports used boxes of different sizes, and a container that fit one company's ships might not fit another's cranes. The benefits of the system depended on everyone adopting {{b:13}} standards, and agreeing on them took years of difficult negotiation. Ports, too, had to be rebuilt. Old harbors in the centers of cities, with narrow piers and little space for storing boxes, gradually lost business to new terminals built on open land, often far from where dockworkers lived.

The human cost of this transition was considerable. In port cities around the world, tens of thousands of dockworkers saw their jobs disappear, and neighborhoods that had grown up around the waterfront went into decline. Labor unions fought the change, and in some places they won agreements that protected existing workers' incomes for many years. But they could not halt the container's {{u:16|relentless}} advance; the savings were simply too large.

Economists have long debated how much the container contributed to the growth of world trade. Its most important effect may have been not the lower cost of shipping itself but the greater reliability it made possible. When manufacturers could count on parts arriving on schedule from distant suppliers, they began to {{b:14}} production across many countries, assembling a single product from components made in a dozen places. In this sense, the humble metal box helped create the global supply chains that define the modern economy — along with the vulnerabilities that became painfully clear when ports were disrupted during the pandemic of 2020.

groups.instruction: 設問A　空所（11）〜（14）に入る最も適切な語句を、それぞれ選択肢 1〜4 から1つ選びなさい。

questions.explanation: トラックの渋滞を「避けよう」としていた。続く「トラックごと船に載せればよい」という解決策とも合う。
「総費用の半分ほども」。量・割合を強調する as much as + 数量。as many as は可算名詞の数に使う。no less は than が必要。
会社ごとにサイズが違って困ったので、全員が「共通の」規格を採用する必要があった。competing（競合する）は逆の意味。
直後「十数か所で作られた部品から1つの製品を組み立てる」から、生産を多くの国に「分散させる（spread）」。

groups.instruction: 設問B　下線部（15）・（16）について、最も適切なものを、それぞれ選択肢 1〜4 から1つ選びなさい。

questions.prompt: （15）下線部が指す内容として最も適切なものはどれか。
choices: the number of boxes carried by the Ideal X
dramatic reductions in the cost of handling cargo
the number of dockworkers who lost their jobs
questions.explanation: 直前の「積み込み費用が1トンあたり約6ドルから約16セントに下がった」という数字を指す。

questions.prompt: （16）下線部の語に最も意味が近いものはどれか。
questions.explanation: relentless は「容赦ない、止まることのない」。労働組合も止められなかった、という文脈とも一致。

groups.instruction: 設問C　本文の内容に照らして、（17）〜（20）の質問に対する答えとして最も適切なものを、それぞれ選択肢 1〜4 から1つ選びなさい。

questions.prompt: Why did McLean first come up with the idea of shipping trailers by sea?
choices: He wanted a faster way to move goods than the crowded roads allowed.
He was asked by the government to improve the port of Newark.
He believed that containers would reduce theft at sea.
He wanted to sell the oil tanker that he owned.
questions.explanation: 第1段落「東海岸の混雑した幹線道路でトラックを遅らせる渋滞を避けようとしていた」。

questions.prompt: According to the fourth paragraph, why did the container not succeed immediately?
choices: Dockworkers refused to lift the boxes.
The boxes were too heavy for most ships.
Container sizes were not standardized, and many ports were unsuitable.
Shipping lines did not believe McLean's cost figures.
questions.explanation: 第4段落: 箱のサイズがばらばらで規格統一に年月がかかり、港も作り直す必要があった。

questions.prompt: According to the last paragraph, what may have been the container's most important effect?
choices: It reduced the cost of shipping.
It made the delivery of goods more dependable.
It created new jobs at ports.
It caused world trade to decline during the pandemic.
questions.explanation: 「最も重要な効果は輸送費の低下そのものではなく、それが可能にした信頼性の向上かもしれない」。reliability = dependability。

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
choices: The Life and Career of Malcom McLean
How a Simple Box Reshaped the World Economy
The Decline of Labor Unions in Port Cities
Why Ports Were Built in City Centers
questions.explanation: コンテナの誕生から普及、世界経済・サプライチェーンへの影響までを扱う文章。1・3・4 は一部の話題にすぎない。

sections.label: III
sections.instruction: 次の英文を読み、設問に答えなさい。解答はマーク解答用紙の 21 から 28 の解答欄にマークしなさい。

paragraphs: For decades, governments and employers tried to encourage people to save for retirement mainly by explaining why it mattered. Workers received brochures, attended seminars, and were shown charts of how small monthly contributions could grow over forty years. The results were disappointing. Many people agreed that they ought to save more, fully intended to do so, and then did nothing. The problem, it turned out, was not a lack of information but a {{b:21}} of action.

Behavioral economists offered an explanation. People tend to stick with whatever option requires no decision — what researchers call the "default." When joining a retirement plan required filling out forms, most new employees put it off, often indefinitely. In one now-famous study, researchers examined a company that changed its rules so that new employees were enrolled automatically unless they chose to {{b:22}}. Participation in the plan jumped from under half of new workers to nearly ninety percent, even though nothing about the plan's benefits had changed.

Findings like this gave rise to the idea of the "nudge," popularized by the economist Richard Thaler and the legal scholar Cass Sunstein. A nudge is any feature of the way choices are presented that predictably changes behavior without forbidding any option or significantly changing financial incentives. Placing fruit at eye level in a school cafeteria is a nudge; banning sweets is not. {{u:24|The appeal to policymakers was obvious}}: nudges were cheap, and they appeared to respect individual freedom while still improving outcomes.

More recent research has added important qualifications. Automatic enrollment raises the number of people who save, but many of them remain at the low default contribution rate chosen by their employer, which may be {{b:23}} too small to provide a comfortable retirement. Some studies also suggest that workers who are enrolled automatically borrow more on credit cards, partly offsetting their new savings. And a large review of nudge experiments found that the effects reported in academic journals tended to be bigger than those observed when the same ideas were tested on a large scale by governments.

None of this means that nudges are useless. It means that the choice of a default is itself a decision with consequences, and that someone must take responsibility for making it well. A carefully designed plan might begin with a modest contribution and raise it automatically each time a worker receives a pay increase — an approach that takes advantage of people's tendency to accept the status quo while gradually moving them toward a more adequate level of saving.

groups.instruction: 設問A　空所（21）〜（23）に入る最も適切な語を、それぞれ選択肢 1〜4 から1つ選びなさい。

questions.explanation: 「貯蓄すべきと分かっていても何もしなかった」ので、問題は情報不足ではなく行動の「欠如・失敗（failure）」。
「自分で〜しない限り自動的に加入」→ unless they chose to opt out（脱退を選ばない限り）。デフォルト（初期設定）の話。
too + 形容詞 を強めるのは far / much。very too は不可。

groups.instruction: 設問B　下線部（24）について、筆者がこのように述べる理由として最も適切なものを、選択肢 1〜4 から1つ選びなさい。

choices: Nudges cost little and still left people free to choose.
Nudges allowed governments to ban unhealthy products.
Nudges were popular among school children.
questions.explanation: コロン以下「ナッジは安価で、個人の自由を尊重しつつ成果を改善するように見えた」。

groups.instruction: 設問C　本文の内容に照らして、（25）〜（28）の英文を完成させる、または質問に答えるのに最も適切なものを、それぞれ選択肢 1〜4 から1つ選びなさい。

questions.prompt: According to the first paragraph, earlier efforts to encourage saving were disappointing because
choices: workers could not understand the charts they were shown.
people did not act even when they knew that saving was important.
questions.explanation: 「もっと貯蓄すべきだと同意し、そのつもりでいながら、何もしなかった」。

questions.prompt: Which of the following would NOT be considered a nudge according to the passage?
choices: Placing healthy foods where they are easiest to see.
Enrolling workers in a savings plan unless they decide otherwise.
Prohibiting the sale of sugary drinks in schools.
Sending people a reminder message before a deadline.
questions.explanation: ナッジは「どの選択肢も禁止しない」ものと定義されている。販売の禁止（banning sweets と同種）はナッジではない。

questions.prompt: According to the fourth paragraph, which is a limitation of automatic enrollment?
choices: It reduces the number of people who join retirement plans.
It is not permitted by law in most countries.
Many enrolled workers continue saving at a low rate.
It cannot be tested on a large scale.
questions.explanation: 「多くの人は雇用主が設定した低い初期拠出率のまま」。2 と 4 は本文に記述なし（大規模な検証は実際に行われている）。

questions.prompt: Which best describes the author's overall view?
choices: Nudges are a complete solution to the problem of low saving.
Nudges have no measurable effect and should be abandoned.
Nudges can be useful, but defaults must be designed with care.
Governments should rely only on financial incentives.
questions.explanation: 最終段落「ナッジが無用なわけではない。初期設定の選び方自体が結果を伴う決定であり、誰かが責任を持つ必要がある」。

sections.label: IV
sections.instruction: 次の（29）〜（38）の英文の空所に入る最も適切な語句を、それぞれ選択肢 1〜4 から1つ選び、マーク解答用紙の 29 から 38 の解答欄にマークしなさい。

questions.prompt: The new regulations, (   ) take effect next April, will affect most small retailers.
questions.explanation: カンマで挟まれた非制限用法の関係代名詞。非制限用法で that は使えない。

questions.prompt: Hardly (   ) the meeting started when the fire alarm went off.
questions.explanation: Hardly had S p.p. when ... 「〜するとすぐに…」。否定語句の文頭で倒置。

questions.prompt: I'd rather you (   ) tell anyone about the merger until it is officially announced.
questions.explanation: would rather + S + 過去形（仮定法過去）で「〜してほしい」。現在・未来のことでも過去形を使う。

questions.prompt: It was not (   ) a customer complained that the manager noticed the error.
questions.explanation: It is not until ... that ~「…して初めて〜する」。

questions.prompt: The company's profits this year are three times (   ) they were five years ago.
questions.explanation: 倍数表現: X times as + 原級 + as。

questions.prompt: (   ) the bad weather, the shipment arrived on time.
questions.explanation: 直後が名詞句なので前置詞 Despite。Although は接続詞なので節が続く。

questions.prompt: After ten years in sales, she is used to (   ) with clients from overseas.
questions.explanation: be used to -ing「〜するのに慣れている」。この to は前置詞。

questions.prompt: Had the central bank lowered interest rates last year, more firms (   ) money to expand.
questions.explanation: If が省略された倒置の仮定法過去完了（Had S p.p.）。帰結節は would have p.p.。

questions.prompt: The unit price of the product varies (   ) the size of the order.
questions.explanation: vary according to ~「〜に応じて変わる」。regardless は of が必要で、意味も逆。

questions.prompt: Not until the 1990s (   ) widely available to ordinary households.
questions.explanation: Not until ... が文頭に出ると主節は疑問文の語順（倒置）になる。

sections.label: V
sections.instruction: 次の会話文を読み、空所（39）〜（43）に入る最も適切なものを、下の選択肢 1〜8 からそれぞれ1つ選び、マーク解答用紙の 39 から 43 の解答欄にマークしなさい。ただし、同じ選択肢を2回以上用いてはいけません。

paragraphs: Ken: Have you seen the sales figures for our first week?
Maria: I have. {{b:39}}
Ken: Better than I expected, honestly. But the reviews keep mentioning the price.
Maria: {{b:40}} We spent months deciding on that number.
Ken: I know. Maybe the problem is how we present it, not the price itself.
Maria: What do you have in mind?
Ken: We could offer a monthly plan as well as the annual one. {{b:41}}
Maria: That's true, though we'd earn less from each customer.
Ken: Not necessarily. {{b:42}}
Maria: Fair point. Let's bring it up at Monday's meeting. {{b:43}}
Ken: Sure. I'll put some slides together over the weekend.

choices: Could you prepare a few numbers before then?
They're not bad for a product nobody had heard of a month ago.
People who start with a monthly plan often switch to the annual one later.
That's a little frustrating to hear.
Paying less up front might feel less risky to new users.
I've never looked at them, to be honest.
Why don't we cancel the launch?
The meeting has been moved to Friday.

questions.explanation: 「見た」と答えた直後で、Ken が「正直、予想より良い」と応じるので、売上への評価を述べる 2。6 は I have. と矛盾。
レビューで価格が指摘されることへの反応。「何か月もかけて決めた」と続くので、不満を表す 4。
月額プランを提案する理由。Maria の「それはそうだが、1人あたりの収益は減る」につながる 5。
「収益が減るとは限らない」の根拠として、月額から年額への移行を挙げる 3。
月曜の会議に向けた依頼。Ken の「週末にスライドを作る」という返事と合う 1。8 は Monday's meeting と矛盾。

sections.label: VI
sections.instruction: 次の（1）〜（7）の英文の空所に、括弧内の語を適切な形に変えて1語で記入しなさい。ただし、括弧内の語をそのまま用いる場合もある。解答は記述解答用紙の所定の欄に記入しなさい。

questions.prompt: The (          ) of the two banks was announced yesterday. (merge)
questions.explanation: 冠詞 The と of の間なので名詞。merge の名詞形は merger（合併）。

questions.prompt: Consumers have become increasingly (          ) of how their personal data is used. (suspect)
questions.explanation: become + 形容詞。be suspicious of ~「〜を疑っている」。

questions.prompt: The firm plans to (          ) its range of products to attract younger customers. (broad)
questions.explanation: to 不定詞なので動詞。broad の動詞形は broaden（広げる）。

questions.prompt: The price of raw materials has risen (          ) over the past decade. (steady)
questions.explanation: 動詞 has risen を修飾する副詞。y → ily。

questions.prompt: The new policy had a number of (          ) consequences that nobody had predicted. (intend)
questions.explanation: 「誰も予想しなかった」から否定の意味。unintended consequences「意図せざる結果」。接頭辞 un- をつける点に注意。

questions.prompt: Online reviews now play a central role in consumers' purchasing (          ). (decide)
questions.explanation: 所有格 consumers' purchasing に続く名詞。purchasing decisions「購買決定」。単数形も可とする。

questions.prompt: The manager insisted that the contract (          ) signed before the end of the month. (be)
questions.explanation: insist that S (should) 原形 の仮定法現在。was ではなく原形 be。

sections.label: VII
sections.instruction: 次の（8）〜（12）の日本語の意味になるように、空所に与えられた文字で始まる最も適切な英語1語を記入しなさい。解答は記述解答用紙の所定の欄に、与えられた文字も含めて記入しなさい。

questions.prompt:
その会社は昨年、多額の負債を抱えて倒産した。
The company went (b          ) last year with huge debts.
questions.explanation: go bankrupt「倒産する」。

questions.prompt:
その製品は需要が供給を上回っている。
Demand for the product (e          ) supply.
questions.explanation: exceed「〜を上回る」。主語が三人称単数・現在なので exceeds。

questions.prompt:
彼女はその提案に強く反対した。
She expressed strong (o          ) to the proposal.
questions.explanation: opposition to ~「〜への反対」。objection to ~ も可。

questions.prompt:
私たちは顧客の期待に応えなければならない。
We must (m          ) our customers' expectations.
questions.explanation: meet expectations「期待に応える」。

questions.prompt:
その政策は長期的には経済に利益をもたらすだろう。
The policy will (b          ) the economy in the long run.
questions.explanation: benefit は動詞で「〜に利益をもたらす」。
